//: Development overrides, merged on top of appsettings.json.

ConnectionStrings.//: EMPTY ON PURPOSE — a credential never belongs in a file that is committed, not even a development one. Supply it from user-secrets, which lives outside the repository and is per-developer. See the README, or run: dotnet user-secrets set "ConnectionStrings:Default" "Server=localhost,1433;Database=TicketHub;User Id=sa;Password=TicketHub!Dev2026;TrustServerCertificate=True;MultipleActiveResultSets=True" --project src/TicketHub.Api
ConnectionStrings.//2: TrustServerCertificate=True is fine for a container on your own machine and is NOT fine anywhere else — it disables certificate validation, which is precisely what stops someone impersonating your database.

Database.//: Logs SQL parameter VALUES. Extremely useful while learning, and a data-protection incident in production — parameters contain email addresses, names and search terms.

Jwt.//: EMPTY ON PURPOSE. Anyone holding this key can mint a valid token for any user, so it is not committed — not even a development one, because development keys have a habit of surviving into production. Set your own: dotnet user-secrets set "Jwt:Key" "<a long random string, 32+ chars>" --project src/TicketHub.Api
Jwt.//2: An hour rather than 15 minutes, so Swagger sessions do not expire mid-exercise. Production should stay at 15.

//3: TIP: set Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.Database.Command below to Information to watch every SQL statement EF generates. Do it once while reading the repository code — seeing the actual SELECT next to the LINQ that produced it is the fastest way to understand what projections and Include really do. (Note: no '//' comment keys inside LogLevel — every key there is read as a category name and an unknown value makes configuration throw.)

RateLimit.//: Deliberately loose in development — 10/minute is not many when you are clicking through a .http file. Production keeps the tight numbers from appsettings.json.
